first.rationale: The visible crisis is competitor entry pricing, which pulls toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 records exactly that intervention as acquisition-positive and 30-day-retention-negative, with an explicit warning not to generalize it. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching discounts would buy volume that churns and would likely worsen the underlying metrics rather than fix them. The two internal signals I can actually move are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and these are causally linked: onboarding completion sits upstream of activation, so a fix there plausibly lifts both, whereas activation_messaging treats the downstream symptom of accounts that already stalled earlier in the funnel. memory_86 (shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value across self-serve) and memory_31 (fewer required signup fields lifted first-week activation) both point the same way. I am verifying memory_86 because it is the memory my action rests on, and memory_91 because activation_messaging is the strongest alternative and I want to know whether its week-one engagement lift reflected durable first meaningful action or a short-lived nudge. I also want the memory_86 source record to check whether it and memory_31 are independent experiments or two consolidations of the same underlying study, since that would mean my evidence base is thinner than the two entries suggest. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: the inherited evidence is consistent but archived and up to two months old, and none of it was gathered under active competitive pressure, so the prior segment mix may not hold. Residual risks I am not resolving this week: onboarding friction may not be the actual cause of the declines if the losses are concentrated in price-sensitive accounts already leaving for the competitor, in which case the lift will be smaller than memory_86 implies; referral_incentive (memory_57) and enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) remain credible but address established and enterprise segments rather than the SMB self-serve funnel where the deterioration is showing.

final.rationale: Both verifications came back confirmed, and neither overturned my prior, but they did narrow the gap between my top two options. exp_86 is stronger than the consolidated summary conveyed: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. That retention number matters most, because the sustainable-revenue objective is precisely where promotional_pricing fails. exp_91 also held up (activation +6%, retention +1%), and it is worth being honest that its +6% activation maps exactly onto the -6% activation decline, which makes it the closest competitor to my choice rather than a clearly inferior option. I am still choosing simplify_onboarding for three reasons. First, onboarding completion is upstream of activation, so a completion fix plausibly addresses both declines while activation messaging addresses only the downstream one and cannot recover accounts that stall before reaching the messaged surface. Second, exp_86 carries the larger retention effect (+3% vs +1%), which is the metric that distinguishes durable qualified revenue from churned volume. Third, the -4% completion decline is direct evidence that the onboarding surface is currently degrading, so the intervention targets an observed regression rather than a general improvement. I explicitly reject promotional_pricing despite it being the most direct answer to the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records that exact play as retention-destroying and carries a standing warning against generalizing it. Matching a discount war would convert a competitive problem into a churn problem and move against the primary objective. The archive did not resolve my independence concern between memory_86 and memory_31. Reading the records, exp_86 is a shortened onboarding flow while memory_31 is reduced signup fields, which look like distinct interventions, but I never pulled memory_31's source and cannot confirm they are not two consolidations of one study. So my evidence base here may be one strong experiment rather than two converging ones. That, plus the fact that all inherited evidence predates the competitor's launch and may not hold under a shifted segment mix, keeps me at standard experiment rather than broad rollout. If the SMB losses turn out to be concentrated in accounts already leaving on price, the onboarding lift will underperform exp_86's numbers. Instrument for completion, activation, and 30-day retention, segmented by price sensitivity, so we learn whether the decline is a friction problem or a competitive-attrition problem. activation_messaging is the clear candidate for the next slot and should be reconsidered first if this underperforms; referral_incentive and enterprise_sales_assist remain credible but address established and enterprise segments rather than the SMB self-serve funnel where the deterioration is actually showing.
